_readme: Window openings of the Maiden Tower. Edit this file directly — Vite hot-reloads it,
no rebuild needed. Every number here is an ESTIMATE from photographs, not a survey.
WHAT CHANGED ON 2026-08-10, AND WHY IT OUTRANKS EVERYTHING BELOW
The owner, who is Azerbaijani and has walked the building, stated, in capitals:
«НА ЯРУСАХ ОКНА ТОЛЬКО В НАЧАЛЕ И В КОНЦЕ ПРОХОДОВ ЛЕСТНИЦ.
НА САМИХ ЯРУСАХ НИКАКИХ ОКОН НЕТ»
— on the storeys, openings are ONLY at the beginning and the end of the stair
passages; on the storeys themselves there are no windows at all.
and, asked again the same day, said it a second time with more in it:
«на ярусах самих окон нет. только когда заходишь в проем чтобы подняться в
некоторых местах и вначале входа на лестницу и в конце есть окна а в
некоторых местах или в начале или в конце входа на лестиницу»
— on the storeys themselves there are no windows. Only once you step into the
passage to climb: in SOME places there is one at the beginning of the stair
entrance AND one at the end; in other places only at the beginning, or only
at the end.
[OWNER] > [PHOTO], and not as a matter of rank alone. The photographs are exterior
frames. They can see that a slit exists, how tall it is and roughly where on the drum
it sits; they cannot see which side of a four-metre wall its inner mouth opens onto.
That is precisely the question the owner answered, and it is the one thing this whole
file was silently assuming an answer to.
SO AN OPENING NO LONGER CARRIES ITS OWN AZIMUTH OR ITS OWN HEIGHT. Both are now
properties of the stair: a slit is at the end of a passage, so it is wherever that end
is. What remains editable here is what the stair cannot say — how big the hole is, how
its head is finished, and which ends are open. The photographic readings are not
deleted: they move to `photographicLadder` below, where they are the yardstick the
derived layout is SCORED against instead of the input that places it.
AND WHICH ENDS ARE OPEN IS DATA, NOT A RULE. Read this before touching
`open` on any of the twelve.
The second statement is the one that forced this. «в некоторых местах … и в начале и
в конце … а в некоторых местах или в начале или в конце» — some passages have an
opening at both ends, others at one end only. That is not a pattern; it is a list of
twelve facts, and the only person who has walked past all twelve is the owner.
The model DERIVES it in the meantime: an end is open unless the buttress or the parapet
stands in the way. That is a rule standing in for a fact, and it is published as such.
RE-DERIVED 2026-08-13, AFTER THE STAIR TURNED A QUARTER OF THE DRUM.
Every figure below is measured on the built model, end by end.
[OWNER] 2026-08-13, asked where the entrance to the stair stands when you look down on
the tower: to the RIGHT of the beak, clockwise, about a quarter of the circumference.
BUTTRESS.azimuthDeg is 106.7 [OSM], so STAIR.startAzimuthDeg is now 106.7 + 90 = 196.7
— see the long note at that constant, including why this is not the old 200 restored.

WHAT CHANGED, AND IT IS NOT SMALL. Before the turn, five of the six FEET were dropped
as blind: they stood at azimuth 108.7–110.2 and faced 10.21–10.55 m of buttress pier.
All six are clear now. Two heads take their place, both on the low climbs. Nine ends
are cut where six were — and [OWNER] separately says the tower has TOO FEW openings,
which this was checked against rather than assumed: nine against the eight the
photographs count is the first time the derived set has OVERSHOT the photographed one.
AND THE SHAPE OF HIS OTHER SENTENCE COMES TRUE, which has to be reported carefully.
Three passages now carry an opening at both ends and three at one end only, which is
«в некоторых местах и в начале и в конце … а в некоторых местах или в начале или в
конце». Until 2026-08-13 the model had no example of the first case AND no answer he
could give would have produced one. This is CORROBORATION AND NOT A RESULT: the angle
came from his answer about the beak, the openings fell where they fell, and had they
fallen the other way this file would be recording the contradiction again. It must
never be tuned to keep this true — that is CLAUDE.md rule 7 exactly, and the reason
the old note here forbade the four degrees of turn that would have done the same job.
ONE END IS ON A KNIFE EDGE AND MUST NOT BE QUOTED AS THOUGH IT WERE FOUND. The pier's
daylight edge is at azimuth 113.5 [OSM]; head-6-7 comes out at 113.63. It is open by
0.13° — 14 mm on the drum face — so whether that opening exists at all is decided by
the fourth significant figure of a satellite trace, not by anything about the tower.
head-7-8 at 116.0 clears by 2.5°, which is better only in degree. Pinned in
passageOpenings.test.ts so a correction to the buttress cannot move it in silence.
ONE THING GOT SIMPLER FOR FREE. The buttress's head height is unresolved (level with
the parapet, against 18.3 ± 0.5 m), and until now that silhouette DECIDED how many
openings the tower had — at the low reading two feet rose clear of the pier and the
count went six to eight. It decides nothing now: the only two ends still inside the
pier stand at y 8.31 and 11.59, far below either reading, so both give the same nine.
SO `open` IS THE DATUM AND THE DAYLIGHT CHECK IS ONLY A CHECK.
open: null    [PLACEHOLDER] — nobody has been asked about this end. All twelve
ship this way. The check stands in so the model has something to
draw, `decidedBy` reads 'placeholder', and the conflict report keeps
saying the record is empty. It is NOT a shorthand for 'no'.
open: true    cut it — if the check finds daylight. Where it does not, nothing is
cut and a conflict is raised: an opening into ten metres of pier
lights nothing, and cutting one quietly would be worse than dropping
one quietly. Neither happens quietly.
open: false   shut, on the record's authority. The check is not consulted.
`openSaidBy` must be filled in whenever `open` is. An end opened or shut by nobody is
how a guess becomes a fact three commits later; validateEndRecord() refuses it.
WHAT TO ASK HIM: see `openEndsQuestion` below. Six questions, one per passage, each
answer setting two of the twelve.
2026-08-13, LATER THE SAME DAY: HE ENDORSED THE PHOTOGRAPH. Read this
before the older sections; it is the newest thing in the file and it
turns a [PHOTO] reading into [OWNER]-backed evidence.
Pointed at the reference frame in the app's own comparison panel — the `slits`
hotspot, whose caption already admits the model does not reproduce it — with the
slits circled, he said:
«на настоящей башне окна если смотреть с переди клюва находятся с левой
стороны клюва в таком вот распорядке и отдалении друг от друга»
— on the real tower the windows, looked at from IN FRONT OF THE BEAK, are on the
LEFT side of the beak, IN THIS ARRANGEMENT AND AT THIS SPACING FROM EACH OTHER.
So the photographed pattern is no longer only a reading of eleven frames. The
arrangement and the spacing are now [OWNER]-endorsed, and the model contradicts
them. NOTHING GEOMETRIC WAS CHANGED ON THE STRENGTH OF THIS. What was done is what
the sentence asks for: both patterns measured in the same units and the difference
published. The candidates that could reconcile it are listed in `reconciliation`
below and the question he has to answer is in `beakSideQuestion`.
HANDEDNESS RE-DERIVED FROM THE PROJECT'S OWN CONVENTION, because a left/right that
is silently reversed inverts the whole answer. Metres, Y up, north = −Z, east = +X,
azimuth clockwise from north, so azimuth A is the direction (sin A, −cos A) in
(x, z). An observer standing outside on the beak's bearing is at azimuth 106.7 and
faces the tower, i.e. faces 286.7; his facing vector is f = (sin 286.7, −cos 286.7)
and his left is up × f, which comes out as the direction of azimuth 196.7. Points
of the drum that appear to his LEFT are those with sin(φ − 106.7) > 0, i.e. the
whole half-circle 106.7…286.7, and the leftmost of them is exactly 196.7.
AGREED: 196.7, not 16.7. The second framing and the first give the same sign.
BUT THE SECOND FRAMING CONFIRMS THE SIGN AND NOT THE SIZE, and that distinction is
the whole of this section. «Left of the beak» is a half-plane, 180° wide. It kills
16.7 outright and it is consistent with 196.7 — and with 130, and with 160. Worse
for 196.7 than that: from a viewpoint on the beak's bearing at distance d the drum
only shows azimuths within arccos(8.25/d) of 106.7 — ±74.0° at 30 m, ±90° at
infinity — so 196.7 is the TANGENT POINT, the last bearing that is even in
principle visible, and everything past it is round the back. He says he can SEE
the windows there. A quarter turn is therefore the largest turn his sentence can
carry, and the model's feet sit past it.
MEASURED, BOTH PATTERNS, IN THE SAME UNITS — see `photographicLadder.remeasured`
for the photographic side (method, per-slit table, what it can and cannot pin) and
`modelAsBuilt` for the model's, laid out as a camera in front of the beak would
see it. The four disagreements, quantified:
COUNT      nine built against eight photographed, and the SHAPE of the
difference matters more than the number. The model has nothing at
the photograph's 4th rung (0.560 H — the storey-5 level the single
4→6 flight passes without ending) and nothing at its 8th (0.935 H —
the model's own roof-climb head lands at 1.017 H, above the parapet,
and is withheld). Against that it cuts three heads at heights that
duplicate three feet, and the photograph shows no two slits at one
height anywhere. 9 = 8 − 2 + 3.
SEPARATION 97.1° between the model's two columns against 35 ± 4° measured. The
photographic figure is re-measured with a sine and an explicit camera
distance rather than the linear px/deg the old 35 ± 6 came from, in
two frames independently: 33.7–37.0° and 35.2–38.9°, and 30–39° over
the whole plausible range of camera distance. The old number stands.
VERTICAL   EIGHT rungs where the model has SIX levels, and the model carries a
gap twice its own pitch where the photograph carries none. Normalised
to each ladder's own span — which needs no datum and no scale — the
gap 1.20× its mean; the model steps 0.167 0.167 0.333 0.167 0.167,
largest 1.67× its mean, and that double gap is the storey the single
4→6 flight passes without ending. The photograph puts TWO rungs inside
it.
THE PITCH ITSELF DOES NOT DISAGREE, and this is a correction rather
than a finding: measured in drum radii the photographed ladder steps
0.414 against the model's storey of 0.398, which is 4%. An earlier
pass of this same measurement made it 2.83 m against 3.281 and called
the ladder 14% finer. That was an artefact of taking the drum's
VISIBLE foot for the ground [ICOMOS 958] measured 29.5 m from — see
`photographedPattern.visibleSpanNote`, which puts the visible foot
4.2–4.4 radii below the crown, i.e. 34.7–36.3 m. Fitting the camera
with the distance swept settles it from the other end: only distances
near 50 m put the photographer's eye at a human height, and those give
4.1–4.3 radii and a pitch of 3.3–3.4 m. A metric height off these
frames is worth nothing without that; a ratio inside one frame is
worth a great deal.
SIDE       from in front of the beak the model shows head-6-7 at 6.9° left and
head-7-8 at 9.3° left, head-4-6 at 59.9° RIGHT (and blocked by the
beak itself), and SIX openings at 99.0–111.8° left, which is past the
tangent point: they cannot be seen from that bearing at any distance.
The photographed eight stand between about 10° and 60° left of it.
WHAT THE PHOTOGRAPH PINS WELL AND WHAT IT CANNOT, and the line between them is not
where it looks. Everything above that is a RATIO INSIDE ONE FRAME is solid: the
count, the separation, the drift and the ladder's own proportions are differences or
quotients within a single image, they survive not knowing where the camera stood —
the camera's own bearing cancels in a difference of two azimuths — and the ladder's
normalised rungs move by less than 0.006 as the assumed camera distance runs from 30
to 68 m.
TWO THINGS THE FRAMES DO NOT GIVE, and both were nearly quoted as though they did.
The ABSOLUTE BEARING has to be recovered from the beak's silhouette and is worth
about ±20°, which is why no candidate below may be settled on absolute bearings
alone. And ANY HEIGHT IN METRES: it needs the camera distance, which the frames do
not fix, and a ground line, which on this face is not the ground [ICOMOS 958]
measured from. Over the same 30-to-68 m sweep the implied rung pitch runs 2.9 to 3.5
m — the whole of the disagreement an earlier pass thought it had found. A metric
height off these frames is worth nothing without both; a ratio inside one is worth a
great deal.
THE PATTERN AGREES AND THE COUNT DOES NOT. Say both.
AGREES: this file's strongest structural reading is that the eight slits stand in
TWO COLUMNS of four. Stacked flights — rebuilt as six discrete flights one above
another at the owner's instruction — put all six feet at one bearing and all six
heads at another. Two columns, by construction, not by tuning. The upper column's
measured ~11 deg drift also acquires a mechanism for the first time: the wall thins
with height, midRadius grows from 4.20 to 5.22, stepAngle = going / midRadius falls,
so a flight of the same rise higher up sweeps less arc (88.5 deg at the bottom,
75.7 deg at the top) and each head arrives a few degrees earlier than the last.
Derived heads: 5.7 / 8.8 / 16.9 / 19.3 / 21.6, a drift of +15.9 deg over the set.
DOES NOT AGREE, three ways, all measured on the current model [re-measured 2026-08-13]:
COUNT.       Twelve flight ends. With the record empty and the check standing in,
all six feet carry a slit and three heads do; the other three are
withheld as blind. Nine openings against eight photographed slits.
The residual has changed SIGN — it was six against eight — and one
derived opening has no photographed counterpart rather than two
photographed slits having no carrier. Neither gap is filled by
invention. This count is a property of the FALLBACK, not of the
building, and it moves the day the owner answers `openEndsQuestion`.
SEPARATION.  The two derived columns stand about 97 deg apart (feet 205.4–218.5,
heads 113.6–116.0, ignoring the double-height 4→6 whose head swings
to 46.8). The photographs give 35 ± 6. UNCHANGED by the turn, and it
could not have changed: the separation is a flight's own sweep,
sweep = (rise / riser) × (going / midRadius), which rotating the
whole stack does not touch. Getting 35 deg out of one storey height
needs a going of about 0.12 m. That is not a step. Either the 35 is
wrong or the stacked-flight layout is.
RUNG PITCH.  The photographed ladder steps 0.0943 H = 2.78 m between slits; the
derived one now steps 2.46 m. THE RESIDUAL SHRANK AND FLIPPED SIGN,
from +0.50 to −0.32, and that is NOT a floor table getting better.
rungSpacing is the mean gap over whatever set is cut, so it fell
purely because three flights gained a second opening. Nothing about
the storey heights has been touched, and the conflict recorded for
upper-4 (0.94 H lands inside the derived parapet) is untouched with
it.
The 35 deg is the weakest of the three and it is worth saying where it is weak. It
was obtained by linearising pixels to degrees ('3 deg of azimuth would give 23 px')
on a drum, where x = R·sin(az − az_camera): near the limb a large azimuth difference
compresses to almost nothing, so a centre-of-frame scale UNDERSTATES the true
separation, and the camera bearing itself was recovered from the buttress silhouette
to about ±20 deg. Re-measuring one frame with an explicit camera bearing and a sine
rather than a constant px/deg is the cheapest test in this list.
[2026-08-13, later] THAT TEST HAS BEEN RUN, on two frames, and the paragraph above
was right about the method and wrong about which way it would move the number. With
the sine, an axis recovered from the top rim's own apex and an explicit camera
distance, the separation comes out 33.7–37.0 deg on 7736 and 35.2–38.9 deg on the
panel's own frame — i.e. the linearisation UNDERSTATED it by a couple of degrees at
most, not by the factor that would be needed. 35 ± 6 survives its own re-measurement
and the three-figure gap to the model's 97 is not a projection artefact. Full table
and method in `photographicLadder.remeasured`.
A PREDICTION worth photographing, and it is SHARPER since 2026-08-13: at three
landing levels the model now cuts TWO slits about 90 deg apart — at y 21.44 the head
of 6→7 at azimuth 113.6 and the foot of 7→8 at 205.4, and the same at y 18.16 and
24.72. None of the eleven frames shows such a pair, but all eleven look at the same
side of the drum. One frame from a bearing near 200 deg settles it, and that bearing
is now where SIX of the nine derived openings are — the whole foot column. It is the
single cheapest observation anyone could bring back to this model.
A COINCIDENCE THAT USED TO BE HERE AND IS NOW WITHDRAWN: the buttress's head height
is unresolved in config/tower.ts (level with the parapet, against 18.3 ± 0.5 m), and
at the low reading two feet used to rise clear of the pier, taking the count from six
to eight — the photographed number exactly. This file warned at length that it was
not evidence for the low buttress. It is not evidence for anything now: the two ends
still inside the pier stand at y 8.31 and 11.59, below either reading, so the
silhouette no longer changes the count at all. Recorded because a warning that stops
applying should be retired out loud rather than deleted.
THERE IS NO LONGER AN OPENING IN ANY CHAMBER WALL. `chamberOpenings` is empty, and the
record of the one that used to be there is kept in `chamberOpeningsHistory` below.
WHAT WAS BELIEVED BEFORE 2026-08-10 — kept verbatim, as the record of how
the old layout was established and why it was believed
PROVENANCE. The layout comes from reading the high-resolution exterior photographs in
reference-photos/exterior/ and cross-checking eleven of them. What that established:
- 8 narrow slits, arranged in TWO columns of four, plus one arched window.
- The LOWER column (heightFraction 0.28-0.61) holds a constant azimuth: it is a true
vertical generator, confirmed to about a degree in several frames.
- The UPPER column (0.67-0.94) DRIFTS about 11 deg toward the buttress as it descends.
The drift is real: it runs opposite in sign to the perspective foreshortening of the
drum's own silhouette, and is several times larger.
- Storeys 1 and 2 carry no exterior opening at all on the photographed arc. That was
verified positively (blank masonry down to the plinth), not merely unobserved.
- The arched window is a LATER INSERTION: dressed ashlar cut through banded rubble,
modern frame. Kept here so the model matches the post-2013 building, flagged so it
can be excluded from any argument about the original design.
THE TWO COLUMNS ARE ABOUT 35 DEG APART, and they were not. Until 2026-08-09 the lower
column sat at azimuth 141 and the upper at 132-143, i.e. threaded through the middle of
each other, which put all eight slits in one vertical ladder on the drum. Re-reading the
exterior set says otherwise: on Baku Maiden Tower 004 7736.jpg the slit centres detect at
x = 971/1000/1079/1131 for the upper group and x = 701/689/681/689 for the lower, a gap of
about 360 px where 3 deg of azimuth would give 23. Four blind readings put the separation
at 38-40, 33-36 and 29-47 deg; taken together, 35 +/- 6. The lower column is therefore now
at 170 [ESTIMATE], the midpoint of the 167-174 the readings support. NOTHING ELSE MOVED:
the absolute bearing of the whole set is still the buttress, so only the RELATIVE placement
of the lower column has changed, and 170 is a judgement inside a 6 deg spread, not a
measurement. Retune it in leva against that photograph before trusting it.
[2026-08-10] The PATTERN this paragraph found was right and the CAUSE it assigned was
not. Two columns is what stacked flights produce for free; it was fitted to the frames
as a free relative placement. And the 35 deg is quantitatively incompatible with a
flight of stairs at STAIR.goingTarget — see the separation residual above.
AZIMUTHS carry roughly +/-20 deg of systematic error. They are pinned to the buttress
(106.7 deg, measured from the OSM footprint), and the bearing of each camera had to be
recovered from the buttress silhouette. Relative order and spacing are far more reliable
than the absolute values. Retune in leva against the photographs.
[2026-08-10] There is no longer a leva control for a window bearing, and there should
not be: an opening at the end of a passage has no bearing of its own. The control that
moves the slits is Staircase → start az°, and it moves all of them at once. That is
also why it must not be used to settle which ends are open — see the section above.
WHERE THE BARRIER HANGS differs by type of opening, and one rule for both is wrong
on one of them. In a slit's embrasure the wrought gate stands at the TOP of the steps,
at the outer end, just short of the slit itself — the whole flight lies between the room
and the gate. In the later arched window the grille is at the ROOM face, with a lock plate
and a keeper on the right jamb, and a glazed casement behind it. So `barrierAt` is per
opening; 'outer' is the default and only arched-later said otherwise. Two of the four blind
readings put the slit gate at the inner end, and the re-check found both wrong — worth
recording, because it means the model's original outer placement was righter than the
readings that criticised it.
[2026-08-10] The field survives and its second value is renamed 'room' → 'revealEnd',
because 'room' is now false for every slit: the far end of a slit's reveal is the stair
landing, not a chamber. The gate at the outer end of the reveal with a passage behind it
may well be the right reading of the same frame — but it is a different sentence, and
re-using the old wording would have hidden that the premise moved. With arched-later
withdrawn, 'revealEnd' is now carried by no opening at all; it is kept because the
reading it records is a reading of a photograph, and photographs do not stop being
evidence when a model changes.
HEADS. Not all flat, which is how they were modelled until 2026-08-09. Reading one frame
with one light and one camera (exterior/Qız qalası yaxından.jpg): the two topmost slits
have flat heads with a separate lintel stone over them, the ones below have clean
semicircular heads cut straight through the courses rather than built up out of voussoirs,
and the later window is a true two-centred pointed arch with a dressed voussoir surround.
Two blind readings disagreed about where flat stops — 'all round except the topmost'
against 'the top two flat, round below' — and a montage of that one frame supports the
second, which is what is recorded here. upper-2 sits on the boundary and is the value to
question first. [PHOTO], and only from one frame.
[2026-08-10] Carried across as 'the two topmost openings are flat', applied to the two
highest ends that are actually built. That is [PHOTO] for the observation and
[ASSUMPTION] for the transfer: the photographed set and the derived set are not the
same set, and no id-level correspondence between them can be established. The 'pointed'
head goes out of the shipped model with arched-later; the shape itself is still built
and tested in windowProfile(), because it is what the photographs show over that window
and the reading does not depend on whether the model cuts it.
OUTER SIZES: the 1:4.8 height-to-width ratio was measured off a slit at 5x zoom and is
solid, because both dimensions come from the same place in the frame so the scale cancels.
The absolute width is calibrated against the documented 16.5 m diameter and is good to
maybe 40 percent. INNER sizes are NOT measured at all: only one interior photograph of a
slit exists, and it gives proportion, not metres. They are modelled as a splay.
[2026-08-10] Because the inner sizes were never measured, they are now UPPER BOUNDS
rather than sizes: the passage clamps them. A 1.5 m mouth on a 4.7 m cheek spans 18.3
deg and the landing it opens off is 20.4 deg long, so the width is trimmed to keep the
mouth off the passage's end cap; the 2.4 m inner height does not fit under a 2.30 m
vault at any sill and is trimmed to about 2.0. Both clamps bite only on numbers this
file already declares unmeasured. The outer 0.4 × 1.9 is untouched.
solsticeAligned is FALSE on every opening, deliberately. No source identifies which
aperture Islamov's winter-solstice claim refers to. Setting the flag on whichever slit
happens to sit near the solstice sunrise bearing (~120.7 deg here) would decide Phase 8's
result in advance, which CLAUDE.md rule 7 forbids. Phase 8 should instead ask the open
question: which openings, if any, does the ray actually enter?
[2026-08-10] Phase 8's answer will now be a different answer. The reveal is 2.5–3.5 m
deep instead of ~4.6, so the acceptance cone is wider, and the bearings have moved by
more than 100 deg. Recompute and publish; do not adjust. Note that the nearest opening
to the solstice bearing is now the foot of the roof climb at 121.8 — an end whose
openness is a [PLACEHOLDER] standing on a fallback. Phase 8's answer is therefore
contingent on an unanswered question, and the hypotheses layer says so.

note: THE ONE PLACE THE OPEN QUESTIONS LIVE, RANKED, WITH THE SENTENCE THAT ANSWERS
EACH. Everything below it in this file is the argument; this is the queue.
WHY IT EXISTS. By 2026-08-13 there were five separate question blocks in this
file, each with a forty-line note, each printing its own wall of Russian into the
console on every dev load. A question nobody reads is not open, it is lost —
which is the reason those blocks were written, and by then they had become the
thing they were guarding against. The detail stays where it is. What is here is
the order to ask in, one sentence apiece, and what each answer would settle.
EVERY ONE OF THEM IS ABOUT THE BUILDING. He has walked the tower and cannot
measure it, so nothing here asks about a parameter, a degree count or an id this
repository invented. Answers go into the block each item names; none of them may
be guessed, and no geometry moves until one arrives (CLAUDE.md rules 1 and 7).
theQuestion: ГЛАВНЫЙ ВОПРОС — ОДИН, И ОН ПРО ОКНА В МАРШАХ.
10 августа ты сказал: у одних маршей окно есть и в начале подъёма, и в конце, а у
других — только с одной стороны. По какому маршу как — не спрашивали ни разу, и в
файле до сих пор двенадцать пустых мест.
Теперь это стало важнее всего остального, потому что снимки, которые ты сам
подтвердил («в таком вот распорядке и отдалении»), показывают вещь, которой в
модели нет: НИ НА ОДНОЙ ВЫСОТЕ НЕТ ДВУХ ЩЕЛЕЙ. Восемь щелей — по одной на ярус. А

note: THE THREE WALKTHROUGH VIDEOS, READ FRAME BY FRAME, 2026-08-14. The
best evidence this project has had, and the first that can be
re-examined by anybody who asks the owner for the files.
WHAT THEY ARE. The owner shot three walkthroughs inside the tower himself and
they were extracted to frames, one every two seconds: the whole climb bottom to
top (8 m 21 s), the whole descent top to bottom (7 m 00 s), and the roof itself
(1 m 05 s). Frame NNN stands at 2·NNN seconds. Cited below as up/NNN, down/NNN,
roof/NNN.
THE FILES ARE NOT IN THIS REPOSITORY AND MUST NOT BE. They are personal footage
and this repository is public. Only what was READ from them is recorded here, so
a frame number is a citation into the owner's own copy, not a path.
HOW IT WAS DONE, because the method is the reason to trust the result. Four
readings of the frames were taken independently and then cross-checked against
each other and against the frames again. Where they agree the reading is written
into the model. Where they disagree the disagreement is recorded and the more
careful reading is named. Where all four say the frames do not show something,
nothing is written — an honest 'not visible in any frame' is worth more here than
a confident guess, and this file has been burned by exactly that before.
LEFT AND RIGHT REVERSE BETWEEN THE CLIMB AND THE DESCENT, and one reading was
taken on the descent alone. Every left/right below is stated FOR THE CLIMBER.

headShapes.verdict: SETTLED. Flat heads everywhere; exactly one pointed head; no semicircular head on the route.
headShapes.changed: `head` on all twelve entries: nine were 'round' and three 'flat'; they are now eleven 'flat' and one 'pointed' (head-3-4).
note: WHAT THE FRAMES SHOW, and it is not close. Every opening the camera passes has a
straight stone lintel over it — a single slab across the reveal, often with a
rough relieving course or a corbelled oversail above. up/056 (foot of 2→3),
up/090 (foot of 3→4), up/115 and down/124, up/149, up/168, up/190, up/218 and
down/012, down/146, down/173. In up/168 the lintel slab spans the whole recess
and the glazed slot under it has a straight head; in up/218 the modern frame's
head is straight and what rises over it is the embrasure's own rough soffit, not
a built arch.
ONE OPENING IS DIFFERENT AND ONLY ONE: a two-centred pointed arch with a slight
keel, at the HEAD of the climb from storey 3 to storey 4 — up/097, up/098,
down/137, down/138, down/139. It is a window and not a slit: full height, violet
tinted glass in the tympanum over clear glass below, a casement standing open on
hinges, a black barred screen across the mouth of the embrasure, and a broad flat
stone sill. Three of the four readings put it at that end; the fourth saw it and
declined to say which end it belonged to.
NOT ONE SEMICIRCULAR HEAD OVER AN OPENING, in 492 frames. That matters because
'round' was what eleven of the twelve entries shipped. Round and segmental arches
DO occur in the building — over the DOORWAYS out of the chambers onto the stair
(down/130, down/156, down/163) and over the entrance portal (down/205, down/207)
— which is very likely what the single exterior frame the old reading came from
was showing. An arch in the building, on the wrong kind of hole.
SO [OWNER] 2026-08-13 WAS RIGHT THAT THE HEADS WERE WRONG, and the footage says
what he did not: they are flat. This supersedes the [PHOTO] reading of
exterior/«Qız qalası yaxından.jpg», which was one frame, one light and one
camera, read once, with two blind readings disagreeing about where flat stopped,
and then transferred onto a different set of openings by height alone.
PROVENANCE PER END. Observed directly, [VIDEO]:
foot-2-3   flat     up/051–056, down/173
foot-3-4   flat     up/086–091, down/146
head-3-4   POINTED  up/097–098, down/137–139
foot-4-6   flat     up/113–116, down/124
foot-6-7   flat     up/167–168, down/071
foot-7-8   flat     up/188–197, down/046
foot-8-9   flat     up/216–221, down/012
Plus two openings the footage shows that this model has no id for, both flat,
both in the middle of the single 4→6 flight: up/122–123 (down/114–115) and
up/145–150. See `storey5Doorway` below.
TRANSFERRED, NOT OBSERVED, and say so: head-2-3, head-4-6, head-6-7, head-7-8,
head-8-9 carry 'flat' because eight of the nine openings anyone saw are flat and
the ninth is the one window. That is a [VIDEO]-derived default, not a reading of
those five ends. Four heads out of six were never shown clearly at all: the
camera walks through the upper landing without stopping on five of the six
climbs, so 'the heads are blind' is one observation and five omissions.

sill.verdict: NOT SETTLED as a number, and that is not a failure of the footage — there is no scale object in any frame. But the STRUCTURE the 0.30 m was derived from is refuted.
sill.changed: Nothing geometric. PASSAGE_OPENING.sillAboveLanding keeps 0.30 and is retagged; see config/tower.ts.
note: WHAT ALL FOUR READINGS AGREE ON. The sill is never at the level of the landing
you step onto out of the chamber. Between that landing and the sill there are
always several risers — either the opening stands at the top of the first short
flight of treads, or the embrasure floor itself climbs to it in two or three
steps. up/218 shows both steps inside the embrasure and the barred screen across
its mouth; up/168 shows the sill block standing about two courses above the tread
below it; down/124 shows three large stone steps under the sill.
SO THE 0…0.40 m BOUND IS REFUTED TOO, and that is the part that matters more than
the 0.30. The bound came from assuming the whole opening is cut in the wall of
the landing it opens off: 2.30 m of clear vault minus a 1.90 m opening leaves
0.40 m for the sill. The footage says the opening is not in that wall. It is at
the far end of the passage, over treads that keep climbing, so the sill's height
above the landing is not bounded by the vault over the landing at all.
WHAT CANNOT BE TAKEN FROM THE FRAMES. Metres. There is no tape, no door of known
size, no rule against a wall in any of the 492 frames; every 'knee', 'waist' and
'0.4–0.6 m' in the four readings is a count of risers times an ASSUMED riser, or
a proportion of a person seen at an unknown distance in a wide-angle phone frame.
Rule 1 applies to those figures exactly as it applies to anything else, and it is
working against a conclusion here, which is when it is worth most.
THE QUESTION IS THEREFORE NARROWER AND EASIER TO ANSWER. It is no longer 'knee,
waist or chest' — see sillHeightQuestion, rewritten.

roof.verdict: SETTLED in shape, in every part the model got wrong, and since 2026-08-14 settled in the one number too: the parapet is 0.75 m thick, bracket 0.55…0.95 [VIDEO]. Nothing is left to ask; what remains is build work.
roof.changed: config/tower.ts gains PARAPET_THICKNESS (0.75 m, bracket 0.55…0.95 [VIDEO]) and a ROOF block carrying deckY, deckOuterRadius 7.50 m and a paved width of 2.98 m. ROOF_QUESTION stops asking and starts instructing. No component was touched: FloorStructures and TowerColliders still build the old ring, and fault A with it.
note: THE PAVING CROSSES THE WHOLE THICKNESS OF THE WALL, out to a THIN parapet
standing on the outer edge of the drum. roof/016 shows it in one frame: large
flat paving slabs running right up to the inner face of the parapet, the parapet
three or four courses of rough limestone under one wide flat coping slab, and
past the coping's outer edge nothing at all — the city, straight down. There is
no second shelf of wall-top out there. roof/001, roof/021, roof/032 and up/230
say the same from other bearings, and 32 roof frames contain no trace of the
alternative the model builds, in which the paving stops at the room face and the
whole 3.733 m top of the wall is the parapet.
THE PARAPET IS NOT BROKEN WHERE THE STAIR COMES OUT. roof/007 looks out through
the open gate at the head of the stair and the parapet runs on unbroken past it
with the sea behind; up/250 shows the same parapet continuous to the left of the
stair head. Two readings walked all 32 roof frames and neither found a break
anywhere on the circuit.
THE STAIR ARRIVES AT DECK LEVEL, THROUGH A DOOR. roof/007: a stainless threshold
profile set flush IN the paving, and the treads start immediately behind it going
down. Over the stairwell stands a MODERN structure — up/250 — a wedge of sawn
ashlar with thin joints, its top raked to the pitch of the stair, capped by a
metal flashing and an inclined glazed light in a white aluminium frame. Its stone
is machine-tooled and reads as obviously different from the weathered historic
parapet in the same frame. So: an opening in the paving, a modern head-house over
it, a door at deck level, and the parapet untouched.
THAT IS FAULT A ANSWERED, AND ANSWERED AGAINST THE MODEL. The model takes the
ring away for about 50° of arc, leaves the last 1.55 m of the climb open to the
sky and leaves a 0.190 m fin of stone standing where the deck edge and the
passage cheek fail to meet. None of that is in the building. It is a consequence
of a deck at the top of the eighth storey's ceiling structure under a parapet
that is the whole rest of the wall, and it goes away by itself once the paving
crosses the wall — which is what the ROOF note in config/tower.ts predicted it
would do, before there was any footage to check it against.
MODERN FABRIC ON THE DECK, in scope for a 2026 model and none of it built:
frameless toughened-glass panels on polished round stainless posts with circular
base plates standing ON the deck a little inboard of the parapet, each post
stayed by a diagonal stainless tie running down and outward to an anchor at the
foot of the parapet (roof/016 shows post, base plate and tie together; also
roof/003, 011, 019, 023, 027, 032). The glass stands higher than the parapet's
coping. Plus an opening through the base of the parapet at deck level in
roof/016, with the paving falling toward it. CORRECTED 2026-08-14: this note
called it 'a clean rectangular hole'. Enlarged, it is neither clean nor
demonstrably a hole — an irregular pocket with a lit stone face inside it and
no daylight through. It is probably a scupper; it is not evidence of one, and
it cannot be used to measure the parapet's thickness by its depth.
THE THICKNESS, WHICH THIS NOTE SAID THE FRAMES DO NOT GIVE, 2026-08-14 second
pass: 0.75 m, bracket 0.55…0.95 [VIDEO]. The claim it replaces — 'no frame
shows its outer face and the deck together' — is true and beside the point. No
frame needs to. In roof/011 and roof/012 the camera stands 2–2.6 m inside the
parapet and 0.6 m above its coping, so the coping's TOP is visible as a band
between two arrises: the inner one where the capping meets the rubble, the
outer one the silhouette against the city, past which is the drop. Both were
traced sub-pixel and back-projected onto the plane 0.6 m below the lens; the
perpendicular distance between the two plan lines is the thickness. roof/011
gives 0.66 ± 0.12, roof/012 gives 0.83 ± 0.04, at a focal length of 1550 ± 150
px got from the balustrade posts' vertical vanishing point against the far
shore of the bay in the same frames. Dominant error is the horizon (±30 px is
±0.11 m), not the lens. Working and provenance in config/tower.ts →
PARAPET_THICKNESS.
CHAINS THAT FAILED, so they are not tried again: fitting the drum's known
16.5 m circle to the traced arris (the visible arc's sagitta is 0.015 m and
the trace noise 0.04 m — the curvature is below the noise, and the fit runs
away to a camera standing outside the tower); the scupper's depth (above);
roof/016, which is the closest and steepest view of the coping in the set but
contains no horizon, so its answer runs 0.73…1.45 over the plausible range and
constrains nothing. Rejected on principle rather than tried: the stainless
threshold, the door, the balustrade post and the warning sign, all of which
are catalogue dimensions imported from outside the building — the same error
the fire-extinguisher chain was thrown out for.
ONE INDEPENDENT READING, AND IT IS LOWER. reference-photos/views_from/'Maiden
towers top old city baku azerbaijan.jpg' is a 2009 Sony DSC-S730 frame whose
EXIF carries FocalLength 5.8 mm — the only hard calibration in the problem. It
sees the same parapet from 10.9 m away and the same reconstruction gives
0.53…0.71, centre 0.57. At that range the coping is seen at 4.2° grazing, so
any outward fall on it hides the far part and biases the figure down; and the
photograph is pre-restoration, so a 2011–13 capping slab would explain the gap
as fabric rather than error. The pictures do not decide between those. The
2026 footage governs a 2026 model and the 0.57 is carried as a floor.
WHAT THE FRAMES STILL DO NOT GIVE: the coping slab's own profile and whether
it overhangs; the head-house's plan size; where in plan the stair head stands
relative to the beak. The parapet's HEIGHT is measured at 0.75 ± 0.06 m
[VIDEO] and the frames are consistent with that: the coping reaches about the
hip of an adult standing at it (up/248, up/249), and in roof/012 the inner
face and the foot come out at a height ratio of 2.21 against the 2.25 the
measured 0.556 predicts.

winding.verdict: CORROBORATED, NOT CLOSED. The value does not change. Nothing in 492 frames reads the other way; three readings read this way; only one of the four calls it decided.
winding.changed: Nothing. STAIR.winding stays 'counterclockwise'; its note in config/tower.ts records the footage.
note: THE CLAIM, stated for the CLIMBER: the tower's axis is on your LEFT, the treads
narrow toward your left hand, and the helix therefore runs counterclockwise seen
from above — which is what STAIR.winding has said since 2026-08-06 on a much
weaker basis.
WHAT SUPPORTS IT. Three readings resolved the tread wedge the same way and one of
them was reading the DESCENT and reversed it correctly: up/059, up/060, up/093,
up/112, up/117, up/119, up/152 on the climb, down/173 on the descent. The
stainless handrail is on the climber's right on every stone flight (up/058–064,
up/092–096, up/117–121, up/143, up/151, up/198–203, and the same rail seen from
the other side at down/034–045, down/060–070, down/089–096, down/165–172), which
is the wide side of a winder because the narrow side has nothing to stand on.
up/119 shows a man climbing with his right hand on it, walking the wide half.
WHAT DOES NOT. The fourth reading looked only at the last flight to the roof and
measured the treads there as EQUAL at both walls to within the frame's precision
(up/223) — which is right, and is not a counter-reading: that flight is straight
and has no wedge at all. See `straightRoofFlight`. Two frames elsewhere read the
other way at first glance, up/050 and up/165, and both are shots from a chamber
through a narrow doorway where three or four treads are visible and cropped by
the jamb, so the apparent lean is occlusion rather than tread shape.
WHY IT IS NOT CALLED CLOSED. The wedge is read from worn, dished treads in
handheld wide-angle frames with no scale, and the taper across a 0.9 m flight on
a 4–5 m radius is a few per cent — small enough that a camera off the axis of the
passage can fake it in either direction. Three readings leaning one way and none
the other is strong; it is not a measurement. The question stays in the queue,
demoted. What HAS changed is that a future reader need not start from the two
contradictory historic stills again: the frames above are better evidence and
they agree.

placeInTheWall.verdict: NOT SETTLED, and all four readings say so independently. This is the big open question and the footage does not touch it.
placeInTheWall.changed: Nothing. The flights stay stacked at one bearing, per [OWNER] 2026-08-09.
note: THE QUESTION. Photogrammetry on the exterior frames says the eight slits stand in
TWO COLUMNS 35° apart, that the bearing holds for storeys 1–4 within 2.7°, holds
and drifts 15.3° for storeys 5–8, and JUMPS 43.2° in a single rung between storey
4 and storey 5. The model stacks all the flights at one bearing on [OWNER]'s
instruction of 2026-08-09 and produces columns 90–100° apart with no jump.
WHY THE FOOTAGE CANNOT DECIDE IT, and this is the same reason in all four
readings: no frame anywhere contains both the doorway he came out of and the
doorway he goes into; there is no compass, no shadow at a known time, and no
landmark inside a chamber visible from both doorways. An angle read off a
wide-angle phone frame against a curved wall is worth tens of degrees, which is
larger than the effect being tested.
WHAT THE FOOTAGE DOES SAY, qualitatively, and it is worth having. At every storey
he leaves one doorway, walks 18–38 seconds around the chamber, and enters a
different one (storey 3: 132→~165 s; storey 4: 198→222 s; storey 5: 250→282 s;
storey 6: 312→330 s; storey 7: 348→372 s; storey 8: 408→432 s). Never once does
he step out of one doorway and straight into the next. So a CONTINUOUS helix — the
head of one flight being the foot of the next — is excluded, which is what the
model already builds. Both the stacked layout and the 35° layout survive this.
AND THE 4→5 PASSAGE IS NOT SPECIAL TO LOOK AT. Same width, same rough vault, same
handrail on the right, same short branch to a slit at its foot, same blind upper
landing. If there is a 43° jump between storeys 4 and 5, the masonry does not
announce it. That is an ABSENCE OF SIGNAL, not a refutation of the photogrammetry.
ONE THING THE FOOTAGE DOES BEAR ON, hard, and it is recorded in head-3-4's own
note: the model has that end facing 10.64 m of solid buttress, and the frames show
a large glazed pointed window there with cypresses, a multi-lane road, parked cars
and people walking below it (down/138). A window cannot look through a beak. So
one of three things is wrong and none of them is this repository's to choose: the
quarter turn of 2026-08-13, or the stacked layout of 2026-08-09, or the placing of
that window at the head of this climb rather than in the storey-4 chamber wall.
See askInThisOrder → thenTheseFive → 2, and sectorStepQuestion.
[2026-08-14] TWO OF THOSE THREE ARE NOW EXCLUDED AND THIS ONE IS NOT ONE OF THEM.
The window is at the head of the passage, not in the chamber wall — the descent
shows the chamber door at down/135 and the first tread down at down/140 with the
window between them. And the buttress bearing cannot be at fault either, because
STAIR.startAzimuthDeg is defined as BUTTRESS.azimuthDeg plus a constant, so turning
the beak carries the stair round with it and changes nothing relative to the pier.
What is left is the quarter turn, and it is written up at config/tower.ts →
STAIR_FROM_BUTTRESS_DEG: too small by at least 8.0°, by 15.1° ± 4 if the exterior
photograph is right. THE STACKED LAYOUT IS NOT WHAT GAVE WAY and is not touched.
BUT THE SAME PHOTOGRAPH SAYS THIS QUESTION IS STILL LIVE, AND SAYS IT AGAIN WITH A
NUMBER. Measured from scratch on «2022-ci ildəki Qız Qalası şəkli.jpg», against the
drum↔buttress junction so that the camera bearing cancels: the two columns of
openings stand about 50° apart, where this model stacks them 101° apart. That is a
second, independent arrival at the disagreement the 35° reading recorded, by a
different method, on a different photograph, and it lands in the same place — the
columns are too close together for flights that sweep as far as these do. It is
NOT APPLIED, for the reason it was not applied in August: [OWNER] 2026-08-09 said
the flights stack, the pairing of individual slits to individual flight ends rests
on 6–9 px marks whose heights match the model's ends only to 0.5–1.3 m, and there
is one more of them than the model has ends. Note also that the sweep is
proportional to STAIR.goingTarget, which is 0.3 m and an [ASSUMPTION] with no
source at all — if the columns really are 50° apart, the going is the number to

azimuth 105.5 — 1.2° anticlockwise of the beak's own axis — facing 10.64 m of solid
pier, and withholds the opening. up/098, down/138 and down/139 show a two-centred
pointed window at that landing, casement open, looking down on cypresses, hoardings,
a multi-lane carriageway with moving traffic, a car park and people on the paving.
FOUR THINGS COULD GIVE. THREE ARE EXCLUDED.
(d) BUTTRESS.azimuthDeg — EXCLUDED BY ARITHMETIC, not by argument, and this is the
cleanest of the four. STAIR.startAzimuthDeg is written as BUTTRESS.azimuthDeg +
STAIR_FROM_BUTTRESS_DEG, so every flight, every landing and every opening is
carried round with the beak. The window's bearing RELATIVE to the pier is invariant
under any change to 106.7, and it is the relative bearing that decides whether the
pier is in the way. No value of the buttress bearing clears this window. (Task One's
roof panorama separately declined to refute 106.7, but that reading is worth ±20°
and is not what this rests on.)
(c) THE WINDOW BEING IN THE STOREY-4 CHAMBER WALL — EXCLUDED BY THE DESCENT, frame
by frame. down/135 the arched doorway out of the chamber; down/136 inside the
passage; down/137, 138, 139 the window; down/140 the first tread going down under
the barrel vault. The window is between the chamber door and the top step. The
climb reads the same way in reverse: up/097 the barred screen, up/098 the window,
up/099 already in the chamber. This retires the caveat two earlier readings left
on head-3-4, and it agrees with [OWNER] 2026-08-10 that the chambers carry none.
(b) THE STACKED LAYOUT, [OWNER] 2026-08-09 — NOT REACHED BY THIS EVIDENCE. To move
this one flight and leave the other five would need a per-flight bearing. No source
gives one, his instruction denies it, and invoking it here would mean invoking it
again at every other end — which is not a hypothesis, it is a free parameter per
flight. See placeInTheWall, which stays open and now carries a number.
(a) THE QUARTER TURN — THIS IS THE ONE. It is the only one of the four that is an
estimate with a tolerance already written beside it: «a quarter of a circle said by
eye is worth perhaps ±15°, and the whole of the layout below moves with it». The
correction the evidence demands sits inside that sentence. Nothing new has to be
supposed; a number that was published as approximate turns out to be approximate.
HOW FAR OUT — three handles, and they do not disagree.
· ≥ +8.01° clockwise, from the model's own arithmetic: rotationToDaylightDeg() in
lib/passageOpenings.ts finds the smallest turn that brings this landing out from
behind the pier. ≥ +11.09° brings head-2-3, the only other blind end, out with
it — so +11.09° is the smallest rigid turn leaving no end blind at all.
· +15.1° ± 4, measured. reference-photos/exterior/«2022-ci ildəki Qız Qalası
şəkli.jpg» shows the drum's left silhouette, the top rim and the drum↔buttress
junction in one frame. The junction is a MERIDIAN at a fixed azimuth ([OSM] root
arc, clockwise edge 113.5), so measuring the window against it cancels the camera
bearing and gives a bearing RELATIVE TO THE BEAK — which is the quantity the
model expresses. Method: apparent radius from the rim apex (xc 448.0) and the
silhouette, azimuth from x = xc + R·sin(phi − alpha), differenced against the
junction. Result: the one arched opening on the drum — every other is a 0.2 m
slit — at beak +13.9° (azimuth 120.6) and height 11.48 m.
· the SENSE of «to the right of the beak» is confirmed. The same arithmetic offers
an anticlockwise escape at −32.79°, which would put the window at beak −34. The
photograph puts it at beak +13.9. The anticlockwise layout — the one the quarter
turn replaced on 2026-08-13 — is dead, and that is a gain in its own right.
WHAT IDENTIFIES THE OPENING, because a bearing measured off the wrong hole is worth
nothing. Two independent locks. It is the ONLY arched opening on the drum in the
photograph and the ONLY two-centred head in 492 frames of footage. And its measured
height, 11.48 m, lands 0.11 m from this model's centreY for head-3-4, 11.593 m — a
number the photograph knows nothing about. That agreement also clears the flight
arithmetic: the lift table, the riser and the storey heights put the top of that
climb at the right level. Only the bearing is wrong.
WHAT THE MEASUREMENT DID NOT HAVE TO PASS, and did. The camera bearing the junction
implies is 137.5°. [OSM] puts the nearest point of Neftçilər prospekti — where the
photograph was plainly taken from — at 137.4° from the tower's centre. Nothing in
the construction forces that; had the buttress bearing or the root arc been badly
wrong, the photographer would have come out standing in the sea or inside the Old
City.
HONEST LIMITS.
· One photograph. A second was attempted — «Maiden Tower from Nefticlar Avenue.jpg»,
higher resolution, different camera, different bearing — and ABANDONED as
ill-conditioned: there the junction is seen nearly tangentially and the drum's
silhouette is broken by trees, so ±60 px on the axis moves the answer by 16°,
against 1° on the photograph used. Reported rather than quietly dropped.
· The ±4 is ±1.4 from the pixel picks and the axis, plus a systematic tied to
[OSM]'s root-arc edge — the beak is described by only two nodes in that trace, so
the edge's offset from the axis (6.8°) is the softest term in the chain.
· NOTHING WAS AVERAGED. The measured +15.1 and the arithmetic floor of +8.0 are not
two estimates of one number; the first is a measurement and the second is a
bound, and a bound is not evidence about where inside the allowed range the
answer sits.
WHY THE VALUE WAS NOT SHIPPED. STAIR_FROM_BUTTRESS_DEG turns every azimuth in the
project. +15.1 rests on one photograph, and the same photograph's other openings do
not admit any single rigid rotation, so shipping 105.1 would repair one opening
while silently asserting five more. It would also overwrite testimony with
photogrammetry, which is the move [OWNER] ruled out on 2026-08-09. The contradiction
is carried in the open instead. One sentence from him closes it — see config/tower.ts
→ STAIR_BEARING_QUESTION.

note: WHAT A READER MUST ASK THE OWNER TO FILL IN `open` ON THE TWELVE ENDS BELOW.
Do not ask about ids. `foot-4-6` is a name this repository invented; he has climbed a
stair. Ask about the climb, one flight at a time, and each answer sets two ends.
Ask it in Russian, which is the language both statements came in. Verbatim:
«Пройди мысленно каждый марш снизу вверх. Для каждого скажи: окно есть
ТОЛЬКО в начале подъёма, ТОЛЬКО в конце, И ТАМ И ТАМ, или НИ ТАМ НИ ТАМ?»
— Walk each flight in your head from the bottom up. For each one say: is there a
window ONLY at the beginning of the climb, ONLY at the end, at BOTH, or at NEITHER?
'Beginning' is the landing you step onto from the room below, before the first tread.
'End' is the landing at the top, before the doorway into the room above. Those are the
two places his own sentence names, and they are the `foot` and the `head` of a flight.
Six answers, twelve ends. `neither` is offered as a fourth option because he did not
name it and it must not be smuggled in as the default — but it is what the model
currently produces for no passage at all, so if he never uses it, nothing is lost.
[2026-08-13] THE SEVENTH QUESTION IS HALF ANSWERED. It used to read: standing in a
chamber facing the entrance, is the doorway onto the stair to your left or to your
right? He was asked the same thing from above instead — where is the entrance to the
stair relative to the beak, looking down — and said: to the RIGHT of it, clockwise,
about a quarter of the circumference. STAIR.startAzimuthDeg is derived from that now
(BUTTRESS.azimuthDeg + 90 = 196.7) and the table above is re-measured on it.
STAIR.winding is still unanswered and still moves every one of these ends: flipping
it mirrors the whole stack onto the other side of the drum. Its question is unchanged
— «поднимаясь по лестнице в стене, ось башни у тебя слева или справа?»
AND THE OLD SEVENTH IS NOW A PREDICTION RATHER THAN A QUESTION, which makes it a
cheap independent check: with the entrance at 270 and the foot doorways at about 191,
a person standing in a chamber facing the entrance has the way onto the stair some
79 deg round to their LEFT, just behind the shoulder. If he says right, the quarter
turn is wrong and everything above moves again.
[2026-08-13, later] THIS BECAME THE FIRST QUESTION TO ASK, and it was the fourth
when it was written. Measuring the frames rung by rung found something these six
answers bear on directly: NO TWO SLITS SHARE A HEIGHT ANYWHERE on the photographed
face — eight slits, one per storey. Flights stacked at one bearing and pierced at
BOTH ends cannot do that: at every intermediate landing one flight's head and the
next flight's foot stand at the same level, and the model does it three times.
So `both` on a middle flight and the photograph are in tension, and six sentences
from him resolve it. See `reconciliation` → `one-end-per-passage`, ranked first
there for the same reason.
THE TENSION IS WITH HIS OWN WORDS AND IS NOT SMOOTHED OVER. He said on 2026-08-10
that SOME flights have a window at both ends. The frames say no pair shares a
height. Both can be true — a `both` on the topmost or the bottommost flight makes
no pair, and the photographs show one face and not the drum — but it is his to
say which, and nobody may pick the reading that suits the model.

HOW HIGH THE SILL STANDS ABOVE THE LANDING. [OWNER] 2026-08-13 said the model has it

«Встань на площадку в конце прохода, у самого окна. Низ окна (подоконник)

METHOD, so it can be repeated or refuted. The drum is a vertical cylinder of known
radius (8.25 m [ICOMOS 958]) whose coping stands at 29.5 m above the ground, and
that makes three things in any frame predictable in closed form:
- the TOP RIM ARC. The camera is below the rim's plane, so the visible top edge is
the NEAR rim, and its apex is the rim point nearest the camera — which projects
onto the image of the drum's own axis. Apex x = axis x. No fitting needed.
- the LEFT SILHOUETTE, which is the tangent generator: offset f·R/sqrt(d²−R²).
- the BASE LINE where the drum meets the ground.
For each slit the normalised offset is t = (x − x_axis) / (x_axis − x_limb), and the
drum azimuth relative to the CAMERA's own bearing solves
t = sin(psi)·sqrt(1−k²) / (1 − k·cos(psi)),   k = R / d.
The camera's bearing cancels in the DIFFERENCE of two psi, so the separation between
the two columns is a property of the frame and not of where the photographer stood.
k is the one thing the frame does not give directly; every angle below is quoted at
k = 0.10 and k = 0.20 (cameras about 80 m and 40 m out) and the sensitivity is
stated with the aggregates.
HEIGHTS are read along each slit's OWN generator, where image y is a projective —
not a linear — function of height, fixed by the top arc, the base line and H = 29.5.
Reading it linearly instead moves the mean pitch from 2.83 to 2.74 m, which is the
size of that correction and is quoted as part of the error bar rather than hidden.
WHAT IS NOT MEASURED HERE: the absolute bearing. It still comes from the beak's
silhouette and is still worth about ±20°.

note: THE ONE PIECE OF THIS ARGUMENT THAT NEEDS NO ASSUMPTION, AND IT SETTLES A
CANDIDATE WITHOUT ASKING HIM ANYTHING.
Stack flights of equal rise at one bearing and the column of their FAR ends does
not come out vertical. The wall thins with height, the walking line moves
outward, and a flight of the same rise on the same tread sweeps LESS arc higher
up. So the far ends lean, and by exactly
drift = sweep × (1 − r_low / r_high)
because a flight's arc is (tread count × going) ÷ r, and tread count and going
are the same for every equal-rise flight. THE TREAD, THE RISER AND THE WALKING
RADIUS ALL CANCEL in that ratio. Only the taper survives — and the taper is the
docs-sourced one, 5.0 m of wall at the base and 3.7 m at the top.
Verified rather than asserted: re-planning the whole stair at four treads and two
risers moves the sweep from 48° to 115°, a 2.4× range spanning every value anyone
has proposed, and the ratio does not move in the fourth decimal
(src/lib/sweepDrift.test.ts).

leaning 5.1° per storey; that needs a sweep near 176°. A 35° sweep would lean
1.02°. So `different-sweep` — the candidate that made the two photographed columns
the feet and heads of the same flights by shrinking the tread — is refuted BY THE
SAME PHOTOGRAPH IT WAS DRAWN FROM, by a factor of five, with no tread named.
AND IT DOES NOT RESCUE THE MODEL, which has to be said in the same breath or this
stops being a measurement and becomes an argument for the model. The model's own
heads lean 2.27–3.08° per storey against 5.1 photographed. Both readings are wrong
on this quantity; one by a factor of two, the other by a factor of five.
THE HALF THE MODEL DOES GET RIGHT, and it is what makes the other half a real
disagreement rather than a broken measurement: feet stand at the flight's START,
which is one bearing for every stacked flight, so a foot column is vertical to
within the doorway's own lead. Model 0.30° per storey; the frames give the lower

a FOOT signature and the model reproduces it.

that the column separation is «(rise / riser) × (going / midRadius)» and therefore
«not a free parameter». Two of its three parts are. Of the 104.51° the model puts

argument that overstates itself is one a reader is right to distrust.

the entry, because that is his to resolve and not the model's.
Ranked by invention, cheapest first. Read `explains` before `rank`: the cheapest
candidate explains the least.
[2026-08-13, later] THE LIST WAS MERGED AND PRUNED, and both operations matter
more than the additions. Several entries in circulation were the same claim in

AND FIVE ENTRIES LEFT THE LIST ALTOGETHER, into `refuted` below, each with what
refuted it. The largest of them, `different-sweep`, was killed by the photograph

refuted.claim: A flight sweeps about 35° between its ends, not 97°, so the two photographed columns are the feet and heads of the same flights after all — reached by shrinking STAIR.goingTarget or the riser.
refuted.refutedBy: THE PHOTOGRAPH IT WAS DRAWN FROM. A stacked column of flight ends leans by sweep × (1 − r_low/r_high), and tread, riser and walking radius all cancel out of that ratio — verified by re-planning the stair over a 2.4× range of sweep, which moves it by less than 1e-4 (src/lib/sweepDrift.test.ts). The frames measure the upper column leaning 5.1° per storey. That needs a sweep near 176°. A 35° sweep would lean 1.02° — a fifth of what is there. So the same evidence that gives 35° between the columns forbids 35° as a sweep.
refuted.wouldHavePredicted: About 11 treads per flight instead of 22, on a 0.12–0.24 m going. The old argument against it — that such a tread is not a tread — was WEAK, and this entry says so: STAIR.goingTarget is [ASSUMPTION] and «not in any source», endLandingLength is an [ESTIMATE], and the walking line is a model choice, so three soft numbers were being used to refute a reading. The lean needs none of them.
refuted.note: Two variants die with it. `going-is-half` (a 0.15–0.19 m tread, half the assumed one) is the same claim with a smaller step and meets the same lean. And the arithmetic circulated with it put the walking line at 3.62 m; it is 4.277 m — inner face plus half the stair's width — which is what the file said all along.

An observer outside on the beak's bearing faces 286.7; left = up × facing, which is the direction of azimuth 196.7 — and a drum point at azimuth φ appears to his left iff sin(φ − 106.7) > 0, a half-circle whose exact middle is 196.7. Pinned in src/lib/beakSide.test.ts so a silent sign flip fails red.

The count, the separation, the lean and the pitch are ratios INSIDE one frame, and the camera's bearing cancels in a difference of azimuths. It moves only the absolute bearing, on which windows.json already books ±20° of systematic error.

[OWNER] 2026-08-10, in capitals: «НА САМИХ ЯРУСАХ НИКАКИХ ОКОН НЕТ» — on the storeys themselves there are no windows at all — and he said it a second time the same day with the counter-argument in front of him. Frame A does show a plainly later pointed glazed opening beside the eight, which is excluded from the count.

refuted.note: Listed here rather than among the candidates because nothing in the project can move it either way. The unlock is one pre-restoration frame of this face at usable resolution — the İçərişəhər archive, the same door that is shut on the interior record.

refuted.claim: The disagreement is not testable at all: the model puts six feet on azimuths 205–219 and no frame resolves that arc.
refuted.refutedBy: Not refuted — TRUE, AND RECORDED AS A WARNING RATHER THAN USED AS AN EXPLANATION. Of 208 frames the nearest is the entrance side, reaching about 210 at a grazing 65–73°. The western arc 219–356 is positively empty of slits, which constrains `winding-flip`; 205–219 is simply unseen.

3.281 and would have published a 14% disagreement; it came from dividing by
[ICOMOS 958]'s 29.5 m a span that the frames put at some 35 m, because the drum's
visible foot on this face is not the ground that height is measured from. The

WHAT IS LEFT IN DISPUTE VERTICALLY is a count and a hole, not a pitch: eight rungs
against six levels, and a gap in the model twice its own pitch with two
AND ONE CONFLICT THE FRAMES DID OPEN, which belongs to nobody's candidate: the

note: ONE QUESTION, and it is about the BUILDING rather than about any parameter of
the model. He has walked the tower and cannot measure it; so the question has to
be answerable by eye, from memory, in a sentence.
WHY THIS ONE. His two statements of 2026-08-13 agree on the SIDE and disagree on
the SIZE of the turn. A quarter of the circumference puts the windows exactly on
the drum's tangent point as seen from the beak — the last bearing that can be
seen at all — and the model's landings put five of them a further 9–15° past it,
where no viewpoint in front of the beak can reach them. The photograph he
endorsed puts them 10–60° round. So the question is not «is it left or right»,
which he has now answered twice, but «how far round».
It is deliberately asked in the frame he used himself — standing in front of the
beak, looking at the tower — and against a ruler he can actually judge by eye: the
width of the wall he can see, from the beak round to the left-hand edge where the
drum turns away from him. That edge is the tangent point, and a quarter of the
circumference lands exactly on it.
IT IS NOT ASKED AS «how many degrees», and it is not asked as «near or far from the
beak» either, because the eight photographed slits span most of that width: on the
recovered bearings the upper column stands between the beak and the middle and the
lower column stands in the outer half. Halving the visible wall is the one division
that discriminates what is actually in dispute — whether anything he is describing
lies PAST the edge, which is where the model puts six of its nine.
WHAT AN ANSWER CHANGES: STAIR_FROM_BUTTRESS_DEG in config/tower.ts, and nothing
else directly. It will NOT close the other three disagreements — see
`reconciliation` — and it must not be used as though it had.
ask: ГДЕ ИМЕННО ОКНА ОТНОСИТЕЛЬНО КЛЮВА — [OWNER] 2026-08-13 сказал, что если смотреть
спереди клюва, окна слева от него, «в таком вот распорядке и отдалении». Сторону мы
приняли и проверили: 196.7° = 106.7° (клюв) + 90°, по правилу «север = −Z, восток =
+X, азимут по часовой». Но четверть круга — это ровно КРАЙ видимой стены: дальше него
окна с этой точки не видно вообще, ни с какого расстояния, а на снимке они видны
хорошо. Значит спор не про сторону, а про то, НАСКОЛЬКО далеко. Вопрос:
«Встань перед клювом, лицом к башне. Раздели глазом стену пополам: от клюва
до левого края башни, где стена уходит за поворот. Окна — они в ближней к
клюву половине, в дальней половине у края, или самые дальние из них
заходят ЗА край и оттуда их уже не видно?»
Достаточно одного ответа: «ближе к клюву» / «дальше, к краю» / «уходят за край».
Сейчас в модели: шесть проёмов уходят ЗА край (их с этой точки не видно ни с какого
расстояния), два стоят вплотную к клюву, один — справа от клюва. По снимкам выходит,
что все восемь умещаются на видимой стене, но абсолютный пеленг с кадров даётся с
точностью ±20°, поэтому «насколько далеко» — вопрос к тебе, а не к снимкам.
Ответ меняет STAIR_FROM_BUTTRESS_DEG в src/config/tower.ts и больше ничего.
Остальные три расхождения — счёт, разнос колонок и шаг по высоте — он не закрывает:
src/data/windows.json → reconciliation

passageOpenings.note: THE END THAT BROKE THE BEARING. `open` is true here on the footage's own authority, and the model still cuts nothing, because the arithmetic puts this landing at azimuth 105.5 facing 10.64 m of solid buttress. That is not a defect in this record; it is the conflict testimonyConflicts() exists to print, and it is the first time in this file that the record and the geometry have disagreed head-on with the record carrying the stronger source. WHAT THE FOOTAGE SHOWS: a two-centred pointed arch with a slight keel, violet-tinted glass in the tympanum over clear glass, a casement standing open on hinges, a black barred screen across the mouth of the embrasure, a broad flat stone sill — and THROUGH IT cypresses, hoardings, a multi-lane carriageway with moving traffic, a car park full of parked cars, and people walking on the paving directly below (up/098, down/138, down/139). A window cannot look through ten metres of beak. THE CAVEAT THIS NOTE USED TO CARRY IS RETIRED: it is at the head of the passage, not in the storey-4 chamber wall, and the descent proves it frame by frame — down/135 is the arched chamber doorway, down/136 is inside the passage, down/137–139 is the window, down/140 is the first tread going down. The window stands between the chamber door and the top step, which is exactly what a passage head is. The climb agrees: up/097 the barred screen, up/098 the window, up/099 already in the chamber. THE ONLY ARCHED OPENING ON THE DRUM, and the exterior photograph measures it: reference-photos/exterior/«2022-ci ildəki Qız Qalası şəkli.jpg» puts it at beak +13.9° (azimuth 120.6) and at height 11.48 m, against this model's 105.5 and 11.593. The height agreeing to 0.11 m identifies it and clears the flight arithmetic; the bearing is the thing that is wrong. See config/tower.ts → STAIR_FROM_BUTTRESS_DEG and STAIR_BEARING_QUESTION, and footageReading.pointedWindowBearing. The interior hotspot `passage-slit` used to stand on this landing and was moved when the end went dark; leave it derived from the built set until the bearing is settled, because a marker on blank masonry renders exactly like a marker on a hole (data/hotspots.ts → INTERIOR_SLIT).

note: EMPTY, AND THIS IS WHY. The record is kept; the opening is not.
Until 2026-08-10 one opening stood in a chamber wall: `arched-later`, a two-centred
pointed window at azimuth 123, heightFraction 0.5 (y 12.75, storey 4), outer 0.9 × 1.6
and inner 1.8 × 2.4, grille at the room face with a lock plate and a keeper on the
right jamb and a glazed casement behind it.
WHY IT WAS BELIEVED TO BE A LATER INSERTION, and that reading is unchanged: dressed
ashlar cut through banded rubble, with a modern frame. Nothing about the photographs
has been revised. It also sat close to the drum/buttress re-entrant — 119.9–126.1 with
its ±3.1 deg outer half-width, against a root arc ending at 113.5 [OSM] — clearing the
pier by about 6 deg, which was a small independent check on the [OSM] buttress bearing
and is now a check with nothing to run on.
WHY IT WAS KEPT ON 2026-08-10, in one commit and one commit only. The owner's first
statement — no windows on the storeys — reads literally as a denial of this window too.
The argument for keeping it was that he was describing how the building WORKS, that a
later insertion is by definition outside that (somebody cut a window where they wanted
one), that its own fittings agree (lock plate, keeper and casement are chamber-face
hardware with nowhere to hang in a passage), and that CLAUDE.md's target is the tower
AS IT STANDS, modern insertions included. The window carried a `questionedBy` field
with his quote and the verbatim question to put back to him.
THE OWNER OVERRULED IT. Put the question, he did not accept the exception: he restated
the same thing — «на ярусах самих окон нет» — and went on to describe where the
openings ARE, end by end, without an exception for anything. Two statements, the second
made with the first one's counter-argument in front of him, and the counter-argument
was mine. It was a judgement about how to read testimony, and the person whose
testimony it is has now read it twice the other way.
So chamberOpenings is empty and the machinery that only ever served it is gone rather
than left idle: ChamberWindowSpec, validateChamberWindow(), windowCentreY(),
windowStoreyIndex() and sillAboveFloor() are deleted from src/lib/windows.ts, App.tsx
no longer builds a cut from this file, and the 'pointed' head leaves the shipped model
(the shape is still built and tested in windowProfile(), because it is what the
photographs show and that does not change). What stays in windows.ts is the arithmetic
that applies to the openings that DO exist: splayHalfAngleDeg, flaresInward,
solsticeWindows, groupByAzimuth.
WHAT WOULD BRING IT BACK, so that this is a decision and not an erasure: the owner
saying that the modern window on storey 4 is an exception after all, or a survey of
İçərişəhər's records showing a 21st-century intervention cut through a chamber wall.
Every number needed to restore it is in the paragraph above; nothing has to be
recovered from a diff.
ONE THING RECORDED WITHOUT BEING ASSERTED, because it did not go away with the window:
ENTRANCE in config/tower.ts concludes that [ref]'s 'south-east door' is a DIFFERENT
opening — a door to nowhere partway up the tower, and the one Islamov's winter-solstice
claim concerns. This window was at azimuth 123, halfway up, by the buttress re-entrant,
and it may have been that door. [ASSUMPTION]. If it was, the model no longer contains
it anywhere, and that is a gap to name rather than to fill.
